rationale: John reports the same saying of Jesus in a different setting: "Now He Himself had testified that a prophet has no honor in his own hometown" (John 4:44, BSB), against Matthew's "Only in his hometown and in his own household is a prophet without honor" (13:57). The wording differs in Greek as well as English: Matthew has ouk estin prophetes atimos ei me en te patridi ("a prophet is not without honor except in the hometown"), John prophetes en te idia patridi timen ouk echei ("a prophet in his own hometown has no honor"; both renderings are this lesson's). John's wording is the same in all eight editions Biblehub lists; Matthew's varies slightly, with "his" added in the Byzantine and Textus Receptus texts and "own" (idia) in Tischendorf. Graded parallel/strong, following conn-matt13-blessed-luke10, where one saying placed in a different scene is graded the same way. That precedent pair is closer in wording than this one; the strong label here rests mainly on John's own attribution of the saying to Jesus ("He Himself had testified"), and neither Gospel cites the other. What is disputed is John's use of it, not the link. John has Jesus go to Galilee after citing it, and the commentators read on Biblehub differ on what "his own hometown" means there: Bengel, Gill and Jamieson-Fausset-Brown say Nazareth, while the Cambridge Bible, following Origen, and Vincent say Judea. Ellicott, on John 4:44, holds that the common geographical answers "are brought to, not from, the text."
